cards.front: Give the two acceptable names for HC≡CH.
cards.back: Ethyne (systematic) and acetylene (common). Both are accepted by IUPAC.

cards.front: How are alkynes named?
cards.back: Like alkenes, but with the suffix -yne instead of -ene. Number the longest chain containing the C≡C so the triple bond gets the lowest number.

cards.front: What is the geometry around an alkyne carbon?
cards.back: Linear, 180°. Each triple-bond carbon is sp-hybridized: one σ bond plus two π bonds join the two carbons.
cards.note: Rotate the model: the four carbons of 2-butyne sit on one straight line.

cards.front: Name this alkyne.
cards.back: 2-Pentyne
sf: Alkyne to name, condensed formula CH₃C≡CCH₂CH₃

cards.front: Name this alkyne.
cards.back: 4-Methyl-2-pentyne
sf: Alkyne to name, condensed formula CH₃C≡CCH(CH₃)₂
cards.note: Number from the end nearer the triple bond: the C≡C gets 2, the methyl gets 4.

cards.front: Name this alkyne.
cards.back: 2,5-Dimethyl-3-hexyne

cards.front: Draw 3-methyl-1-butyne.
How can an alkyne be made from a vicinal dihalide?
cards.back: By two consecutive dehydrohalogenations (two E2 eliminations) with a strong base, usually sodium amide, NaNH2. Each step removes one H and one X.
cards.note: The intermediate after the first elimination is a bromoalkene (a vinylic halide).

cards.front: Predict the product.
cards.back: 1-Butyne.
cards.note: This dibromide comes from 1-butene + Br<sub>2</sub>. So an alkene can be turned into an alkyne in two stages: add Br<sub>2</sub>, then eliminate twice.

cards.front: Making a terminal alkyne this way uses 3 equivalents of NaNH2 and an NH4Cl workup. Why?
cards.back: Two equivalents do the two eliminations. The terminal alkyne is acidic, so the third equivalent removes its ≡C–H, giving the alkynide anion. NH4Cl then puts the H back.

cards.front: Predict the product.
cards.back: Cyclohexylacetylene: geminal dihalides also give alkynes by double elimination.

cards.front: Predict the product.
cards.back: Diphenylacetylene, after two eliminations of HBr.

cards.front: How many times does Br<sub>2</sub> add to an alkyne?
cards.back: Once or twice, depending on how many equivalents are used. One equivalent usually gives the trans dihaloalkene; a second gives the tetrahaloalkane.

cards.front: Predict the product. Show the stereochemistry.
cards.back: (E)-2,3-Dibromo-2-butene: the two Br atoms add anti, so they end up trans.

cards.front: Predict the product.
cards.back: 2,2,3,3-Tetrabromobutane.

cards.front: Predict the product.
cards.back: 2-Bromo-1-hexene (Markovnikov).

cards.front: Predict the product.
cards.back: 2,2-Dibromohexane: a geminal dihalide.
cards.note: Both additions are Markovnikov, so both Br atoms end up on the same carbon.

cards.front: HX + alkyne: how many additions, which regiochemistry, and what kind of dihalide?
cards.back: One or two additions, depending on the molar equivalents of HX. Both are Markovnikov, giving a geminal dihalide.

cards.front: Predict the product.
cards.back: 2-Hexanone, a methyl ketone.
cards.note: Markovnikov addition of water gives an enol, OH on C2. The enol tautomerizes to the ketone.

cards.front: In Hg2+-catalyzed hydration of 1-hexyne, what is formed first, before the ketone?
cards.back: An enol: an OH on a C=C carbon. It quickly isomerizes to the ketone.

cards.front: What are keto–enol tautomers?
cards.back: Constitutional isomers that interconvert easily with a trace of acid or base. An H moves between O and C, and the double bond shifts between C=O and C=C.

cards.front: Why do most aldehydes and ketones exist mainly in the keto form?
cards.back: The C=O double bond is stronger than the C=C double bond of the enol.
cards.note: Cyclohexanone contains only about 0.0001% of its enol tautomer at room temperature; acetone contains even less.

cards.front: Draw the enol tautomer of cyclohexanone.
An enolate anion is protonated. Where can the proton add, and what does each give?
cards.back: On oxygen → the enol. On carbon → the keto form. The two are formed reversibly and interconvert.

cards.front: Predict the product.
cards.back: Hexanal, an aldehyde.
cards.note: Anti-Markovnikov: the OH goes on the terminal carbon, and that enol tautomerizes to an aldehyde.

cards.front: Predict the product.
cards.back: Phenylacetaldehyde.

cards.front: Predict the product.
cards.back: Acetophenone, a methyl ketone.

cards.front: Predict the product.
cards.back: Butane: two equivalents of H<sub>2</sub> add.
cards.note: Pt, Pd or Ni reduce the alkyne all the way to the alkane; the reaction does not stop at the alkene.

cards.front: Predict the product. Show the stereochemistry.
cards.back: trans-4-Octene, (E).
cards.note: A dissolving-metal reduction: net anti addition of hydrogen, giving the trans alkene.

cards.front: Predict the product. Show the stereochemistry.
cards.back: cis-2-Butene, (Z).
cards.note: Syn addition of H<sub>2</sub> on the catalyst surface. The catalyst is deactivated, so it stops at the alkene.

cards.front: What is Lindlar’s catalyst, and what does it make?
cards.back: Palladium on CaCO3, deactivated (“poisoned”) with lead acetate and quinoline. It hydrogenates alkynes only as far as the cis alkene.

cards.front: 2-Butyne is reduced two ways. Which reagent gives which alkene?
cards.back:
H2, Lindlar → cis-2-butene (syn).
Li or Na in NH3 or an amine → trans-2-butene (anti).
cards.note: Rotate each model: in the cis isomer both CH<sub>3</sub> groups are on the same side of the C=C.

cards.front: Why does Li in ethylamine give the trans alkene?
cards.back: Li donates one electron to the π bond (radical anion), which takes H+ from the amine (vinylic radical). A second Li gives a vinylic anion, which prefers the less crowded trans shape before it is protonated.

cards.front: Predict the product. Show the stereochemistry.
cards.back: (Z)-2,3-Dideuterio-2-pentene.
cards.note: Both D atoms add to the same face (syn), so they end up cis.

cards.front: Predict the product.
cards.back: Butylbenzene.
cards.note: Both the C=C and the C≡C are reduced. The benzene ring is not reduced under these conditions.

cards.front: What do O<sub>3</sub> and basic KMnO<sub>4</sub> do to an internal alkyne?
cards.back: They cleave the triple bond, turning each alkyne carbon into a carboxylic acid: R–C≡C–R′ → RCO2H + R′CO2H.
cards.note: It works, but it is not the best way to make carboxylic acids; better methods come in later chapters.

cards.front: Predict the products.
cards.back: Acetic acid + propanoic acid.

cards.front: An alkyne, C6H10, gives only propanoic acid with O3 then HOAc. What is it?
cards.back: 3-Hexyne.
cards.note: A symmetrical alkyne: both halves are CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>C.

cards.front: Give the approximate pKa of the C–H in ethyne, ethene and ethane.
cards.back: Ethyne ≈ 25 · ethene ≈ 44 · ethane ≈ 50. Acetylenic hydrogens are far more acidic than other C–H bonds.

cards.front: Rank from most to least acidic: H–NH<sub>2</sub>, H–OH, H–C≡CR, H–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, H–OR, H–CH=CH<sub>2</sub>.
cards.back: H–OH (15.7) > H–OR (16–17) > H–C≡CR (25) > H–NH2 (38) > H–CH=CH2 (44) > H–CH2CH3 (50)

cards.front: Why is a terminal alkyne C–H so much more acidic than an alkene or alkane C–H?
cards.back: The anion’s lone pair sits in an sp orbital, which has 50% s character. It is held closer to the nucleus and is more stable than an sp2 or sp3 anion.

cards.front: Predict the products.
cards.back: Sodium propynide (an alkynide) + NH<sub>3</sub>.

cards.front: NaNH<sub>2</sub> deprotonates a terminal alkyne, but NaOH does not. Why?
cards.back: NH3 (pKa 38) is a much weaker acid than the alkyne (25), so the equilibrium lies on the alkynide side. Water (15.7) is a stronger acid than the alkyne, so hydroxide can’t pull the proton off to any useful extent.

cards.front: What is an alkynide (acetylide) anion?
cards.back: The anion R–C≡C:– formed when a strong base removes the ≡C–H proton of a terminal alkyne. It is a strong base and a good nucleophile.

cards.front: What is alkylation, and why does it matter?
cards.back: A carbon–carbon bond-forming reaction that lengthens the carbon chain. Reactions that make C–C bonds are some of the most important in organic synthesis.

cards.front: In an alkyl halide, which carbon does the nucleophile attack, and why is it δ+?
cards.back: The carbon bonded to X. The electronegative halogen polarizes the C–X bond, leaving that carbon partially positive.

cards.front: What is a leaving group?
cards.back: A substituent that can leave as a relatively stable species, either as an anion (e.g., Br–) or as a neutral molecule.

cards.front: What is steric hindrance?
cards.back: When the spatial arrangement of atoms or groups at or near a reacting site blocks or slows a reaction.

cards.front: Rank these by how fast a nucleophile attacks C–X: methyl, 1°, 2°, 3°, neopentyl.
cards.back: Methyl > 1° > 2° ≫ neopentyl > 3°
cards.note: Approximate relative rates: methyl 30, 1° 1, 2° 0.03, neopentyl 0.00001, 3° ~0. Tertiary and neopentyl carbons are too hindered to react.

cards.front: Which alkyl halides work in acetylide alkylation?
cards.back: Methyl or primary halides that are unbranched at the second carbon. More hindered halides don’t work.

cards.front: Predict the product.
cards.back: 2-Pentyne.

cards.front: Predict the product.
cards.back: Propyne.

cards.front: Predict the product of all three steps.
cards.back: 2-Methylpentane.
cards.note: Alkylation gives 4-methyl-2-pentyne; hydrogenation then gives the alkane. Alkynes are handy for building other functional groups.

cards.front: What is retrosynthetic analysis?
cards.back: Planning a synthesis by working backward from the target molecule to simpler starting materials. Often several routes are possible.

cards.front: Work backward: which terminal alkyne and which alkyl halide make this target?
cards.back: Cyclohexylacetylene (deprotonated with NaNH<sub>2</sub>) + bromoethane.
cards.note: Break the bond between the alkyne carbon and the CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>: the alkynide is the nucleophile, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br the electrophile.

cards.front: Give the reagents and intermediates for this conversion.
cards.back: (1) NaNH<sub>2</sub> (2) CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br (3) Li in C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> or Na in NH<sub>3</sub>
cards.note: Trans alkene, so finish with a dissolving-metal reduction, not Lindlar.

cards.front: Give the reagents and intermediates for this conversion.
cards.back: Alkylate, reduce to the alkene, then hydrate.
cards.note: 3-Hexene is symmetrical, so H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, oxymercuration or hydroboration all give 3-hexanol.

cards.front: Starting from acetylene and any alkyl halide, make 2-heptanone.
cards.back: Alkylate once, then Hg<sup>2+</sup> hydration.
cards.note: Markovnikov hydration of a terminal alkyne gives the methyl ketone.

cards.front: Starting from acetylene and any alkyl halide, make this alkene.
cards.back: Alkylate twice with benzyl bromide, then reduce.
cards.note: Benzyl bromide is a primary halide, so it alkylates well. Use Lindlar instead of Li in the last step for the cis alkene.

cards.front: Starting from acetylene and any alkyl halide, make 1,2-dichloropropane.
cards.back: Alkylate, reduce to the alkene, add Cl<sub>2</sub>.

cards.front: Starting from acetylene and any alkyl halide, make acetic acid.
cards.back: Alkylate twice with CH<sub>3</sub>Br, then cleave.
cards.note: Symmetrical 2-butyne splits into two identical acetic acid molecules.

cards.front: Starting from acetylene and any alkyl halide, make 2-bromopentane.
cards.back: Alkylate, reduce to the alkene, add HBr.
cards.note: Markovnikov HBr addition puts Br on C2. (Adding HBr directly to 1-pentyne would not work: it gives a bromoalkene, then a gem-dibromide.)

cards.front: Which reagents add to an alkyne twice if you use enough of them?
cards.back: X2 (→ tetrahalide), HX (→ gem-dihalide) and H2 with Pt, Pd or Ni (→ alkane).

cards.front: How can you stop at the alkene stage?
cards.back: One equivalent of X2 or HX · H2, Lindlar for the cis alkene · Li or Na in NH3/amine for the trans alkene

cards.front: A terminal alkyne is hydrated two ways. Which gives a methyl ketone and which an aldehyde?
cards.back:
H2O, H2SO4, HgSO4 → methyl ketone (Markovnikov).
BH3·THF; then H2O2, OH– → aldehyde (anti-Markovnikov).

cards.front: You want to lengthen a carbon chain using an alkyne. What are the two steps, and what limits the halide?
cards.back: (1) NaNH2 to make the alkynide; (2) an alkyl halide, which must be methyl or primary and unbranched at the second carbon.
